questions: Do any of your close blood relatives have a similar tremor or shaking?
Does drinking a small amount of alcohol noticeably reduce your tremor?
Do you have any history of liver disease, jaundice, or hepatitis?
Does the tremor continue even when your hands are completely relaxed at rest in your lap?
Have you noticed any problems with your balance, walking, or coordination?
Have you or your family noticed any changes in your speech (e.g., slurring or scanning)?
Do you have any history of psychiatric symptoms, depression, or behavior changes?
Have you been diagnosed with any thyroid problems, or do you have heat intolerance, weight loss, or palpitations?
Are you currently taking any prescription medications, supplements, or recreational drugs?
Did the tremor begin gradually or did it appear suddenly?
Has anyone in your family died from a young-onset liver or neurological disease?
Do you have any difficulty with handwriting, drinking from a cup, or other fine motor tasks when you are not under stress?
orders: Repeat the spiral drawing and the arm-holding task to look for a kinetic/postural tremor that worsens with goal-directed movement.
Ask the patient to drink a glass of water and observe the cup-to-mouth trajectory for worsening of the tremor on approach.
Test for rebound by having the patient flex the arms against resistance and then suddenly releasing, to look for cerebellar hypometria.
Test finger-to-nose and heel-to-shin coordination to assess for cerebellar dysfunction.
Assess rapid alternating movements (dysdiadochokinesia) of the hands.
Test tandem gait (heel-to-toe walking) to look for truncal ataxia.
Draw a straight line on paper and have the patient attempt to follow it with a pen to assess intention tremor.
Write a short sentence (e.g., "Today is a good day") to assess writing and micrographia.
Check visual acuity and perform a fundoscopic examination to look for optic atrophy or retinopathy.
Check serum ceruloplasmin level.
Check 24-hour urinary copper excretion.
Check serum copper level.
Check liver function tests (AST, ALT, bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, albumin, INR).
Check a complete blood count to look for anemia, leukopenia, or thrombocytopenia.
Check serum electrolytes, BUN, and creatinine.
Check thyroid function tests (TSH and free T4).
Check serum glucose to rule out hypoglycemia as a contributor.
Check blood alcohol level if there is any suspicion of acute intoxication.
Order a non-contrast MRI of the brain with attention to the basal ganglia, thalamus, and cerebellum.
Order a slit-lamp examination to look for Kayser-Fleischer rings.
Order nerve conduction studies and electromyography (EMG) if peripheral neuropathy is suspected on examination.
Consider a liver biopsy if Wilson disease remains strongly suspected and non-invasive testing is inconclusive.
Consider a percutaneous liver copper quantification as part of the liver biopsy if performed.
Consider genetic testing for ATP7B mutations if Wilson disease is confirmed or highly likely.

dx_raw:
DIAGNOSIS: Kennedy disease (X-linked spinobulbar muscular atrophy) due to a pathogenic CAG trinucleotide repeat expansion in the AR (androgen receptor) gene

Alternatives:
1. Hirayama disease (juvenile monomelic amyotrophy) with bilateral C7–T1 involvement
2. Essential tremor with an incidental motor neuronopathy at C7–C8
3. Juvenile-onset amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (lower motor neuron–predominant)
